newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels rely on peasant collaboration in jungle.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels rely on peasant collaboration in jungle.

text.p: An arthritic old woman steps out of a wooden jungle shack to feed her pigs and sees a young man in battle fatigues sitting on a rusty oil drum. He cradles a rifle in his lap.
"Just resting," he tells her, and continues idly whistling a revolutionary hymn in the still air.

The woman carries on with her farmyard chores. Then she goes inside to prepare the lean guerrilla an evening meal -- pasta soup and coffee. Later she makes him a bed for the night but the rebel declines the offer saying he must move on.
The collaboration of poverty-stricken peasants is vital for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) in its jungle heartland in the mountains of central Peru, an MRTA leader told Reuters.
"If it were not for the villagers' collaboration, we could not exist," said "Comrade Alejandro," who said he was a member of the MRTA's high-command.

Over 200 miles (300 km) away in Lima, jungle-trained MRTA guerrillas are holding 72 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence, which they stormed in a dramatic bid to free 400 comrades locked up in Peruvian prisons.
The hostage-takers live off sushi dishes and other meals brought in to the diplomatic mansion by the Red Cross.
But in the jungle area where the eastern slopes of the Andes meet the Amazon rain forest, the rank-and-file of MRTA rebels depend on what fare peasants can provide.

Travelling for two days with a 10-man MRTA unit for 30 miles (50 km) by truck and foot, a Reuters correspondent saw peasants provide rebels with food, lodging and transport. They also helped sneak packages past army check-points.
Alejandro said some cooperated purely out of fear. But he claimed 70 percent of the villagers helped because they supported the movement and its avowed fight against poverty.
President Alberto Fujimori's government insists the MRTA is simply a band of common criminals with no support base that extorts villagers and forces then to join their movement.

Analysts say the group started off in the mid-1980s as a Robin Hood-style band robbing trucks to distribute food to the poor, but quickly lost sympathy with Peruvians due to its increasingly bloody bombing and kidnapping campaigns.

One taxi-driver -- pressed into service to take a rebel into the hills from a low-lying river village -- received adequate payment to cover his gasoline costs, but complained he would be in trouble with the army.
"If they ask me, I'll say, 'They force us,' which is true. We're defenceless," he said before engaging the rebel in a debate over the hostage negotiations in Lima.

An hour and a half away by truck along a mud track, a teenage fruit picker said he cooked for up to 15 MRTA rebels about once a month. "You do it out of goodwill because they only come when they are hungry," said the farmhand, who asked not to be named.
But he lived on the side of a road with frequent patrols and said he was petrified the army would discover him.
Alejandro said MRTA guerrillas -- estimated to number no more than 200 -- tried to reduce the risk for the villagers and avoided putting them in compromising positions.

"Many have gone to prison. It (helping us) is a risk that they know exists. At the end of the day we have weapons to defend ourselves with. They don't. So we have to ensure they are not put in trouble," he said.

For two days, the rebels moved with ease through the jungle and made no attempt to hide themselves as grandmothers and young children alike watched them with a blank gaze. Greetings were a nod of the head or a handshake.

Juan, the trainer of the 10-man unit, said the MRTA's rank-and-file spent so much time in the communities expounding their Marxist doctrine, it was not uncommon for rebels and villagers to fall in love. "Do you think sentiment would not grow, with us always among them?" he asked.
But with Fujimori stung by the hostage crisis and vowing to wipe out the MRTA, the rebels and their peasant helpers are never too far from danger.
In the yard where the old woman fed the young rebel, the boredom of the long night wait was abruptly broken when a car appeared on the edge of the clearing.
The rebel crouched down, fixed his stare at the headlights and trained his AKM gun straight at the driver. But it turned out to be the owner of a small farm nearby.
"You never lose the habit. It could always be the enemy."
